15.0.0.en: Azariah: Uzziah (2 Chr 26:1). At the death of Amaziah his son Azariah succeeded him on the throne, as was stated before in the previous chapter (v. 21), and that was in the twenty-seventh year of Jeroboam II king of Israel. The age of Azariah at that time was sixteen years, and his reign lasted fifty-two years, and Jerusalem was the capital of his kingdom. The name of his mother was “Jecholiah,” of Jerusalem.

15.0.1.en: But it is to be noted that Amaziah died in the fifteenth year of the reign of Jeroboam (ch. 14:17), and so there is a period of twelve years between the death of Amaziah and the reign of his son Azariah, because Azariah began to reign in the twenty-seventh year of Jeroboam. During these twelve years Uzziah was king but a child, and a council of regency was the one that managed the kingdom. In the sixteenth year of Azariah the regency ended and Azariah ruled alone for fifty-two years, that is, he died at the age of sixty-eight.

15.1.0.en: He followed the steps of his father Amaziah in doing what was right, but the matter of offering sacrifices to God on the high places remained as it was, and the people continued to offer and burn incense on them.

15.1.1.en: It is beautiful that King Azariah did what was right in the eyes of the Lord, and this is due to two things:

15.1.2.en: 1- His mother was from the kingdom of Judah, from Jerusalem, and it seems that she held fast to the worship of the Lord.

15.1.3.en: 2- The council of regency over the child king Azariah most likely played a good role in leading the kingdom in the worship of God, and so the king, when he came to rule alone at the age of sixteen, continued the worship of God and did what was right in His eyes.

15.2.0.en: After Azariah was able to build cities and lead his kingdom successfully, he became proud, so that he entered the Holy Place, which may be entered only by the priests, and the Lord struck him with leprosy (2 Chr 26:16-21), and he was confined in a separate house, because he was a king, instead of dwelling in a tent outside the walls of the city (Lev 13:46). With the isolation of Azariah in the house of the sick, the throne became vacant, and Jotham the son of Azariah reigned in the lifetime of his father, and then the reign of Jotham extended another sixteen years alone. The books of Amos and Zechariah mention an earthquake in the days of Azariah (Amos 1:1; Zech 14:5), and most likely this earthquake occurred when the king dared to enter the Holy Place to burn incense on the altar of incense, and God struck him with leprosy.

15.3.0.en: The rest of the acts of Azariah are all written in “the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah.”

15.4.0.en: Azariah died and was buried with his fathers in the city of David, and his son Jotham took the throne after him. It is not mentioned that he was buried in the tombs of the kings, and perhaps that was because of his leprosy, which remained with him until the end of his life, and this disease represents uncleanness.

15.4.1.en: Pride lowers a person’s dignity and loses him the care of God, and so he is afflicted with many troubles. So why, my brother, do you attribute the glory to yourself when you achieve success? Thank God and glorify Him, and your success will increase, and you will keep your humility and remain in joy.

15.5.0.en: Zechariah the son of Jeroboam took the throne of Israel; he represents the fourth and last generation of the descendants of Jehu who ruled Israel, exactly as the Lord said to Jehu, to the fourth generation (2 Kgs 10:30). His taking the throne was in the thirty-eighth year of Azariah king of Judah. He reigned in Samaria, and his rule lasted only six months.

15.5.1.en: After the death of Jeroboam II, civil conflicts arose that delayed Zechariah’s sitting on the throne of the kingdom for some years, most likely twelve years, and then Zechariah reigned after that.

15.6.0.en: Zechariah continued in his evil lusts, such as the worship of the gods of the surrounding pagan nations and various works of uncleanness, in addition to the worship of the idols that Jeroboam the son of Nebat had set up; therefore God allowed him to reign only six months, because of the multitude of his evils.

15.7.0.en: Shallum the son of Jabesh plotted a conspiracy and killed King Zechariah, and then reigned in his place.

15.7.1.en: Shallum reigned by a conspiracy and the killing of another, and works that rest on treachery, betrayal and evil of course anger God and expose their doer to many troubles. So do not use any wrong means to achieve your aims, because the end does not justify the means. Be godly in your goals and also in your means, and rely on God, and He will support you in all your steps.

15.8.0.en: The rest of the affairs of Zechariah and his acts are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel.

15.9.0.en: What happened was a fulfillment of the word of the Lord, which He had said before to Jehu, the founder of the ruling house, which continued to sit on the throne of Israel to the fourth generation, that is, the descendants of Jehu, who were Jehoahaz, then Joash, followed by Jeroboam II, and in the end Zechariah.

15.10.0.en: A full month: what is meant is one month, that is, thirty days.

15.10.1.en: Shallum is the one who rebelled against Zechariah the son of Jeroboam (v. 10) and killed him and seized the throne of Israel for himself. His reign began in the thirty-ninth year of Uzziah king of Judah, and his rule lasted only one month.

15.10.2.en: God hates violence and hardness of heart, so do not hasten toward it, lest violence strike you also. And do not use your power to achieve your interests against the commandments of God, because God is able and is the avenger of the blood of His servants.

15.11.0.en: Tirzah: a large city lying in the north of Ephraim. It was a capital of Israel in ancient times, before the time of Omri king of Israel, who founded Samaria.

15.11.1.en: It seems that parties had formed within the kingdom of Israel during the period when the throne of the kingdom was vacant after Jeroboam II, so that although Zechariah reigned, one of the parties rose up and killed the king and Shallum reigned in his place, and then another party, centered in Tirzah, rose against King Shallum and killed him, and Menahem reigned in his place.

15.12.0.en: The rest of the affairs of Shallum and the details of the conspiracy that he led are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel.

15.13.0.en: Tiphsah: modern Tiphsah, lying ten kilometers southwest of Nablus (Shechem). Menahem attacked Tiphsah and its surroundings and destroyed what was in it, as far as the border of Tirzah, because its inhabitants had shut the gates of the city in his face and had not opened its gates to him. He was not content to destroy the city, but committed atrocities against its people, for he ripped up its women with child, and that was because the city of Tiphsah was loyal to King Shallum and his party.

15.14.0.en: When Menahem seized the throne of Israel after killing Shallum the son of Jabesh, it was in the thirty-ninth year of Azariah king of Judah. The capital of his kingdom was Samaria. And he reigned ten years.

15.15.0.en: Menahem walked in evil and the worship of idols, like Jeroboam the son of Nebat, throughout the period of his rule, and in this he led his people astray and led them in the worship of idols and unclean lusts.

15.16.0.en: A talent of silver: it had various weights ranging from twenty to forty kilograms. During his reign Pul king of Assyria came invading. Menahem worked to avoid his attack on the land of Israel by giving him a thousand talents of silver to confirm him on the throne, and in this Menahem became a slave of the king of Assyria, that is, he could reign only under the protection of the king of Assyria.

15.16.1.en: The Lord did not overlook the extreme cruelty with which Menahem treated the inhabitants of the city of Tiphsah. So He brings a nation from afar to punish Menahem for his evil deeds. God neither slumbers nor sleeps, and He repays evils to those who do them.

15.17.0.en: The shekel of silver: the ordinary shekel is 5.8 grams and the shekel of the sanctuary is 11.6 grams.

15.17.1.en: He imposed a sum of fifty shekels of silver on every man, collecting it from the wealthy, to pay it to the king of Assyria to appease him. So the king of Assyria turned back and did not occupy the land of Israel. But he returned afterward and attacked the kingdom of Israel, and this was the beginning of the Assyrian attacks, which ended in the complete captivity of the kingdom of Israel.

15.18.0.en: The rest of the accounts of Menahem and all that he did are written in the “book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel.”

15.19.0.en: Menahem died and was buried with his fathers, and his son Pekahiah succeeded him.

15.20.0.en: Inheritance was not the normal situation for the kings of Israel, but it continued for a period with the descendants of Jehu to Zechariah; then the kingship became again a matter of violence, that is, each one killing his predecessor, until Menahem, who died, and his son Pekahiah inherited the kingship after him; his capital was Samaria and his reign lasted two years, and the beginning of the reign of Pekahiah was the fiftieth year of King Azariah of Judah.

15.21.0.en: Pekahiah continued in evil like his father Menahem, that is, the worship of idols, lusts and injustice, and he persisted in the worship of the idols that Jeroboam the son of Nebat had set up, and in this he led his people in the worship of idols and every evil.

15.21.1.en: If you are in a position of responsibility or a leader, beware; for your sins greatly affect those around you, and they imitate you and so you draw them away from God. The sin of stumbling others is a great sin, and the Lord Christ affirms that its punishment is destruction, so be careful in your conduct, and if you err, apologize, and if you notice that someone has stumbled, explain to him and care for him, so that you do not draw him away from God.

15.22.0.en: A captain: a great commander very close to the king, the third who rides with the king in his chariot.

15.22.1.en: Pekah the son of Remaliah was a great commander close to King Pekahiah, and he had power in the kingdom, so he was considered its real mover. He was strong in character, as shown by the fact that his reign lasted twenty years afterward, and he had a political opinion, which was independence from Assyria, because Menahem and his son Pekahiah had submitted to Assyria and paid it tribute. Pekah allied himself with Rezin king of Aram to break away from Assyria and tried to bring Ahaz king of Judah in with him, but the latter refused. And when he found that Pekahiah did not want to break away from Assyria, Pekah rose against him and killed him and killed two of his aides, Argob and Arieh. In this conspiracy Pekah had with him fifty men of the Gileadites, and perhaps Pekah was from Gilead; therefore he sought the help of the Gileadites, and so the conspiracy was carried out and Pekahiah died, and Pekah the son of Remaliah reigned in his place.

15.23.0.en: The rest of the acts of Pekahiah during the period of his rule are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel.

15.24.0.en: Pekah’s installing himself as king over Israel was in the fifty-second year of Azariah king of Judah. He reigned in Samaria and his rule continued twenty years, but Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria reigned eighteen years and was a contemporary of Pekahiah and Pekah and, after him, Hoshea, kings of Israel. So the period of twenty years is not the period of his rule on the throne of Israel, but was during the former kings Pekahiah and Menahem and before them, since he was a commander in the army and the real force moving the kingdom.

15.25.0.en: He did all the evils that his fathers had done before and did not refrain from walking in the ways of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who drew Israel after him to spiritual and moral destruction.

15.26.0.en: Ijon: a fortified city of the children of Naphtali in the northern part of Palestine. It is now the village of Dibbin in southern Lebanon, near Marj Ayoun.

15.26.1.en: Abel-beth-maachah: a fortified city in Naphtali. Its place today is “Tell Abel,” a village west of the Jordan. Janoah: a city in Naphtali, the present “Yanuh,” ten kilometers east of Tyre. Kedesh: a fortified city of Naphtali in Galilee, now the village of “Qadas,” sixteen kilometers north of Safed.

15.26.2.en: Hazor: it was the capital of the Canaanites in northern Palestine. It lay above the waters of Merom.

15.26.3.en: It was given to the tribe of Naphtali. At present it is “Tell al-Qadah,” about six kilometers west of the Bridge of the Daughters of Jacob.

15.26.4.en: Gilead: a mountainous region east of the Jordan.

15.26.5.en: Galilee: a province in the mountainous region of Naphtali.

15.26.6.en: The land of Naphtali: in the northern part of the land of Palestine, bounded on the east by the Sea of Tiberias and the Jordan, and on the west by the land of Issachar and Zebulun.

15.26.7.en: The First Book of Chronicles tells us (1 Chr 5:26) that the kings of Assyria Pul and Tiglath-pileser attacked the tribes of the children of Israel, the Reubenites and the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh, and took their cities and carried them away captive and transported them and scattered them throughout the Assyrian kingdom. And it tells us here in this verse of another attack of Tiglath-pileser on the tribe of Naphtali, and he took from it the lands mentioned here and seized them and scattered their inhabitants in the cities of Assyria, so they became slaves in captivity.

15.26.8.en: We understand from this that Assyria’s taking of the kingdom of Israel came in three stages. We mentioned two stages here; as for the third stage, they occupied the rest of the cities of Israel, and the northern kingdom ended after King Hoshea, who followed King Pekah.

15.26.9.en: Satan your enemy keeps attacking you until you fall into his hand, so do not submit to him if he fights you, but take refuge in God quickly and resist him, and he will flee from you, and be sure that the power of God which is with you is stronger than Satan, so do not be troubled by your weakness.

15.27.0.en: Conspiracy came to prevail again, and Hoshea the son of Elah rebelled against Pekah the son of Remaliah and assassinated him and seized the throne of Israel in the twentieth year of Jotham the son of Uzziah.

15.27.1.en: What is meant by the twentieth year is from the beginning of the reign of Jotham, and it is to be noted that Jotham reigned only sixteen years, that is, four years after the death of Jotham.

15.28.0.en: The rest of the acts of Pekah are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel.

15.29.0.en: Jotham ascended the throne of Judah, succeeding his father Uzziah. That was in the second year of Pekah the son of Remaliah king of Israel, because Pekah reigned in the last year of the reign of Uzziah (v. 27) and in the following year, that is, the second year, when Uzziah died, his son Jotham reigned. It should be noted that this is the sole reign of Jotham, but it was preceded by several years in which he reigned with Uzziah his father, because of his leprosy and his isolation from dwelling in Jerusalem.

15.30.0.en: Jotham was twenty-five years of age when he became king, and his rule in Jerusalem lasted sixteen years. His mother was Jerusha the daughter of Zadok.

15.30.1.en: We notice here, as we mentioned before, how great is the influence of a godly mother on her children. For the very next verse tells us the conduct that Jotham followed, for he did all that was right.

15.31.0.en: Jotham cared to keep the commandments of God and His worship and walked uprightly before Him, as his father Uzziah had walked, and learned from him to live with God, but he guarded against the errors of his father, which were pride and entering the altar of incense in the Holy Place among the priests.

15.32.0.en: Among the good works of Jotham was not only his holding fast to the commandments and the worship, but he also cared for the Temple of God, and so he built the higher gate, which was most likely a gate facing the north side of the Temple, through which came the animals that were to be slaughtered for God. But among the errors of Jotham is that, like most of the kings of Judah, he let the people sacrifice on the high places and did not limit sacrifice to the bronze altar of the Temple of God.

15.33.0.en: The rest of what Jotham did is written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah, which is not the Book of Chronicles found in the Holy Bible. But the Second Book of Chronicles (2 Chr 27) tells us that Jotham cared to build many buildings beside the Temple and also cared for the fortifications of Jerusalem, because of the danger of an attack by Aram or Assyria.

15.33.1.en: Know that every good work you do is very precious to God, so be careful to do good and help the needy and care for the house of the Lord.

15.34.0.en: At the end of the days of the rule of Jotham, Aram began to ally itself with Israel to make war on the kingdom of Judah, and although King Jotham was good, the people were corrupt and did not submit to the king (2 Chr 27:2); therefore the Lord wanted to chastise them, and so He allowed Aram and Israel to begin military skirmishes and they moved toward the kingdom of Judah, but no complete actual war took place until after the death of Jotham and the reign of his son Ahaz; for God, for the sake of the goodness of Jotham, postponed these attacks to the age of his son, the wicked King Ahaz.

15.34.1.en: And in this we notice the goodness of Jotham for the following reasons:

15.34.2.en: 1- The godliness of his mother Jerusha, who cared to bring him up well.

15.34.3.en: 2- His concern to do what is upright, by keeping the commandments and the holy acts of worship.

15.34.4.en: 3- He cared for the Temple of God, and so he built the higher gate of the Temple and set up many buildings on the high place beside the Temple.

15.34.5.en: 4- He cared to fortify Jerusalem, that the kingdom of Judah might be strong before the attacks of enemies.

15.34.6.en: 5- He guarded against the errors of his father, and so he was humble and did not try to break the Law and enter the Holy Place. As for the errors of Jotham, they appear in the following:

15.34.7.en: 1- His permitting and continuing the offering of sacrifices to God on the high places.

15.34.8.en: 2- He was occupied with building works instead of bringing up his sons, and so Ahaz his son turned out wicked, and when he reigned evil prevailed in the kingdom, and perhaps Jotham married a wicked wife, the mother of Ahaz, who helped in the going astray of her son.

15.35.0.en: Jotham died and was buried with his fathers in the city of David, and his son Ahaz reigned in his place. Ahaz king of Judah
